title: Cap. X Ultimum Propos. 2: why not to all need not trouble the believer who holds just condemnation in Adam; Epist. 107 — Grace of God is not given to all men
latin: Cur autem non omnibus detur, fidelem movere non debet, qui credit ex uno omnes isse in condemnationem justissimam. Ne nimis multus sim in accumulandis testimoniis, illud unicum adjungam quod exstat Epistola cvii. in qua, inter duodecim illas sententias quae ad fidem Catholicam pertinere affirmat, haec secunda est, Gratiam Dei non dari omnibus hominibus.
pass_a: But why it is not given unto all ought not to move the believer, who believes that from one all went into most just condemnation. Lest I be too lengthy in heaping up testimonies, I will add that one alone which stands in Epistle 107, in which, among those twelve sentences which he affirms to pertain unto the Catholic faith, this second is, That the grace of God is not given unto all men.
pass_b: Why it is not given to all need not trouble the believer who holds that from one all went into most just condemnation. Not to pile witnesses: I add only Epistle 107, where among twelve sentences he affirms belong to catholic faith, the second is: The grace of God is not given to all men.

title: Cap. X Ultimum Propos. 2: Epist. 107 means regenerating, sanctifying, saving grace—not Arminius’s common illuminating grace; nor ‘given because they willed’
latin: Quae verba, ne Arminio quidem arbitro, ad illam illuminantem, excitantem, et suadentem gratiam sunt referenda; (nam illam facit omnibus mortalibus communem) sed ad regenerantem, sanctificantem, et salvantem. Neque hic abdere se possunt in illud latibulum, Hanc gratiam vivificantem et salvantem dari de facto quibusdam, quia voluerunt illam accipere; non dari aliis, quia voluerunt respuere. Nam in illa ipsa Epistola Pelagianum habetur, statuere, hanc gratiam dari nobis quia volumus; Orthodoxum per hanc gratiam Deum efficere ut velimus. Huc adde, Hanc esse hujus gratiae conditionem ac virtutem, ut nullo duro corde respuatur, quia in hoc datur ut cordis durities primitus auferatur.
pass_a: Which words, even Arminius being judge, are not to be referred unto that illuminating, exciting, and persuading grace; (for that he makes common unto all mortals) but unto regenerating, sanctifying, and saving. Neither can they here hide themselves in that lurking-place, That this vivifying and saving grace is in fact given unto certain ones, because they willed to receive it; not given unto others, because they willed to refuse it. For in that same Epistle it is held Pelagian to establish that this grace is given unto us because we will; Orthodox that by this grace God effects that we will. Add hither, That this is the condition and virtue of this grace, that it is refused by no hard heart, because it is given unto this end, that the hardness of heart be first taken away.
pass_b: Those words—even Arminius judging—do not point to illuminating, exciting, persuading grace (which he makes common to all mortals), but to regenerating, sanctifying, saving grace. Nor can they hide here: that vivifying, saving grace is in fact given to some because they willed to take it, and withheld from others because they willed to refuse. In that same epistle it is Pelagian to hold this grace is given because we will; Orthodox that by this grace God makes us will. Add: this grace’s condition and power is that no hard heart refuses it, because it is given first to take hardness of heart away.

lemmas.gloss: Epist. 107 = saving not common illuminating grace

title: Cap. X Ultimum Propos. 2: Prosper — God foresaw whom he would give to believe; liberating grace prepared for some, not others; saving grace passes some by
latin: Ab Augustino non dissentit Prosper: Ad Excerpt. Gen. dub. 8. Agnoscamus, inquit, sapienter pieque fateamur; praescisse incommutabiliter Deum quibus esset daturus ut crederent, aut quos daturus esset Filio suo, ut ex eis non perderet quemquam. Et hanc esse praedestinationem sanctorum, praescientiam scilicet et praeparationem gratiae Dei qua certissime liberantur. Caeteros autem, quicunque non liberantur, quos a generali perditione humani generis gratia non exemit, justo noverimus judicio non exemptos. Ponit gratiam liberantem praeparatam et donatam aliquibus; negat eandem praeparatam aut donatam aliis. Et in libro De ingratis, cap. 12. Pelagianum dogma habetur, Quod gratia Christi Nullum omnino hominem de cunctis qui generantur Praetereat. Et de vocatione Gentium, lib. 2. cap. 13. diserte asserit, Salvantis gratiam aliquos praeterire.
pass_a: Prosper does not dissent from Augustine: Ad Excerpt. Gen. dub. 8. Let us acknowledge, he says, and wisely and piously confess that God immutably foresaw unto whom he would give that they should believe, or whom he would give unto his Son, that he might lose none of them. And that this is the predestination of the saints, namely the foresight and preparation of God’s grace by which they are most certainly freed. But the rest, whosoever are not freed, whom grace has not exempted from the general perdition of humankind, let us know by just judgment not exempted. He lays down liberating grace prepared and given unto some; he denies the same prepared or given unto others. And in the book De ingratis, cap. 12. it is held a Pelagian dogma, That the grace of Christ Passes by no man at all of all who are born. And De vocatione Gentium, lib. 2. cap. 13. he expressly asserts that The grace of the Saviour passes some by.
pass_b: Prosper agrees with Augustine (Ad Excerpta Genovensium, dub. 8): Let us wisely and piously confess that God immutably foresaw to whom he would give belief, or whom he would give to his Son so as to lose none of them—and that this is the saints’ predestination: foresight and preparation of the grace by which they are most certainly freed. The rest, not freed, whom grace did not exempt from humankind’s general perdition, we must know by just judgment not exempted. He sets liberating grace prepared and given to some; he denies it prepared or given to others. In De ingratis 12 the Pelagian dogma is that Christ’s grace passes by no one born; and De vocatione Gentium 2.13 he expressly asserts that the Savior’s grace passes some by.

title: Cap. X Ultimum Propos. 2 close: Milevis and Orange preach justifying/converting inspiration not given promiscuously to all — Synod of African exiles in Sardinia
latin: Verum ad Concilia transeamus, de quibus illud generatim affirmare licet, Gratiam Christi talem in illis praedicari, qualem omnibus non dari promiscue clamat ipsa experientia. Milevitanum, Gratiam Dei per Jesum Christum nobis donatam, gratiam justificationis esse, declarat, can. 3, 4, et 5. Hanc autem (quicquid de excitante et illuminante gratia statuatur) non esse omnium communem nemo dubitat. Eadem est sententia Arausicani, quod docet hanc gratiam de qua nunc quaeritur, esse inspirationem Spiritus sancti corrigentem voluntatem nostram ab infidelitate ad fidem, ab impietate ad pietatem, Can. 5. Talem autem ac tam efficacem inspirationem aliquibus dari, aliquibus non dari, adeo manifestum est, ut non inscitiae solum, sed stultitiae sit illud negare. Denique, habemus optimum et maxime expressum testimonium in Epistola Synodica Episcoporum in Sardinia exsulantium. Sic igitur illi; De gratia non digne sentit, quisquis eam putat omnibus hominibus dari. Paulo post ostendunt quam gratiam intelligunt, nempe eam quae in homine operatur et velle et facere. Pergunt, atque explicant insuper in quibus Dei gratia hoc operatur; Hoc, inquiunt, operatur in suis, ut suam salutem operentur. Sed quinam tandem sunt illi quos Deus pro suis agnoscit? Mox sequitur; Omnes praedestinati ipsi sunt quos Deus vult salvos fieri. Ex quibus omnibus consequitur, Esse aliquos quibus nec data nec destinata unquam fuit haec gratia efficax ad salutem.
pass_a: But let us pass unto the Councils, of which one may generally affirm that Such a Grace of Christ is preached in them as experience itself cries out is not given promiscuously unto all. Milevis declares that The grace of God given unto us through Jesus Christ is the grace of justification, can. 3, 4, and 5. But that this (whatever be established concerning exciting and illuminating grace) is not common unto all, no one doubts. The same is the sentence of Orange, which teaches that this grace of which we now inquire is the inspiration of the Holy Spirit correcting our will from unbelief unto faith, from impiety unto piety, Can. 5. But that such and so efficacious an inspiration is given unto some, not given unto others, is so plain that to deny it is not ignorance only but folly. Finally we have an excellent and most express testimony in the Synodical Epistle of the Bishops exiled in Sardinia. Thus therefore they; He does not think worthily of grace, whosoever thinks it is given unto all men. A little after they show what grace they mean, namely that which works in a man both to will and to do. They go on, and explain further in whom God’s grace works this; This, they say, it works in his own, that they may work their own salvation. But who at length are those whom God acknowledges as his own? Presently it follows; All the predestinated themselves are those whom God wills to be made safe. From all which it follows that There are certain ones unto whom this grace efficacious unto salvation was never either given or destined.
pass_b: Turn to the councils: in them such a Grace of Christ is preached as experience itself cries is not given promiscuously to all. Milevis declares (can. 3–5) that the grace of God given through Jesus Christ is the grace of justification—and no one doubts that this (whatever is said of exciting and illuminating grace) is not common to all. Orange teaches the same (can. 5): the grace now in question is the Holy Spirit’s inspiration correcting our will from unbelief to faith, from impiety to piety. That such efficacious inspiration is given to some and not others is so plain that to deny it is folly, not mere ignorance. Best and most express is the Synodical Letter of the bishops exiled in Sardinia: He does not think worthily of grace who thinks it is given to all men. A little later they name the grace they mean—the one that works in a man both to will and to do—and add: This it works in his own, that they may work their salvation. Who are those God owns? Presently: All the predestined themselves are those God wills to be saved. So some never had this grace efficacious to salvation given or destined to them.

lemmas.lemma: nec data nec destinata ... gratia efficax
lemmas.gloss: Sardinia exiles: some never destined saving grace

title: Cap. X Ultimum Propos. 2→3 bridge: Orthodox consent — regenerating Grace of Christ not to all but to God’s peculiar own; Propos. 3 opens on mere mercy without prior person-difference
latin: Videtis jam ex consensu Orthodoxorum, Gratiam Christi proprie dictam, hoc est, regenerantem et salvantem, non dari omnibus, sed certis personis quas pro suis Deus peculiariter vendicat. Restat ultima propositio, quae causam maxime continet, quaeque apud omnes Orthodoxos non minus in confesso fuit, quam duae priores. Illa gratia Christi quae constat infusione fidei, charitatis, atque omnium donorum ad salutem infallibiliter efficiendam necessariorum, (hoc est, quae sanat animam, quae dat bonum velle et perficere) non datur hominibus ex antecedaneo intuitu ad meliores aliquas operationes aut dispositiones accipientium, neque negatur aliis ex antecedaneo intuitu ad pejores illorum operationes aut dispositiones non accipientium, sed ex mera Dei voluntate miserentis cujus vult, et cujus non vult non miserentis, absque omni respectu ad praevium discrimen personarum.
pass_a: Ye see now from the consent of the Orthodox that the Grace of Christ properly so called, that is, regenerating and saving, is not given unto all, but unto certain persons whom God peculiarly claims as his own. There remains the last proposition, which most contains the cause, and which among all the Orthodox was no less in confession than the two former. That Grace of Christ which consists in the infusion of faith, charity, and of all gifts necessary unto infallibly effecting salvation, (that is, which heals the soul, which gives to will the good and to accomplish it) is not given unto men from antecedent regard unto some better operations or dispositions of the receivers, nor denied unto others from antecedent regard unto their worse operations or dispositions as non-receivers, but from the mere will of God showing mercy on whom he wills, and not showing mercy on whom he wills not, without any respect unto a previous discrimination of persons.
pass_b: From Orthodox consent you see: the Grace of Christ properly so called—regenerating and saving—is not given to all, but to certain persons God peculiarly claims as his. The last proposition remains, which most holds the cause, and which all the Orthodox confessed no less than the two before. That Grace of Christ which consists in infusing faith, charity, and every gift needed to effect salvation infallibly—that is, which heals the soul and gives to will and finish the good—is not given from prior regard to some better acts or dispositions in the receivers, nor denied from prior regard to worse acts or dispositions in non-receivers, but from God’s mere will of mercy on whom he wills and non-mercy on whom he wills not, with no respect to a prior difference of persons.

lemmas.lemma: non dari omnibus, sed certis personis
lemmas.gloss: regenerating grace to God’s peculiar own
Propos. 3: mere mercy without prior person-difference

title: Cap. X Ultimum Propos. 3: catholic doctrine — opposite always Pelagian/Semipelagian badge; they grant common offered mercy but make healing grace hang on prior merit
latin: Hanc fuisse doctrinam Catholicae Ecclesiae patet, 1. Quia contraria semper a Pelagianis et Semipelagianis defensa fuit, et ejus ea quasi proprium insigne habita. Nam utcunque (quod etiam Arminiani jam faciunt) gratiam quandam agnoverint ex mera Dei misericordia omnibus oblatam, tamen illam quae sanat, vivificat, et justificat, quaeque non offertur tantum ex parte Dei, sed jam possidetur ex parte hominis, illam, inquam, cenrebant datam nisi ex antecedente merito bonae alicujus operationis aut dispositionis quam in accipiente vidit Deus, in aliis non vidit.
pass_a: That this was the doctrine of the Catholic Church is plain, 1. Because the contrary was always defended by the Pelagians and Semipelagians, and held as it were their proper badge. For although (as the Arminians also now do) they acknowledged a certain grace offered unto all from God’s mere mercy, yet that which heals, quickens, and justifies, and which is not only offered on God’s part, but is already possessed on man’s part—that, I say, they thought given only from antecedent merit of some good operation or disposition which God saw in the receiver, and did not see in others.
pass_b: That this was catholic church doctrine is plain, first because the contrary was always the Pelagians’ and Semipelagians’ defense and as it were their badge. Though (as Arminians also now do) they granted a grace offered to all from mere mercy, yet the grace that heals, quickens, and justifies—and is not only offered by God but already possessed by man—they thought given only from antecedent merit of some good act or disposition God saw in the receiver and not in others.

lemmas.gloss: healing grace hung on prior disposition

title: Cap. X Ultimum Propos. 3: Augustine on Pelagius — grace to the worthy; Prosper’s chronicle; Faustus — attracting mercy if given to the worthy
latin: Sic de Pelagio ipso scribit Augustinus, eum nempe tenuisse, donare Deum hanc gratiam ei qui fuerit dignus accipere, Cap. 14. De gestis Palaestinis. Et Haer. 88. idem Pater testatur Pelagianorum errorem fuisse, Quod gratia Dei qua liberamur ab impietate, secundum merita nostra detur. Sic etiam Prosper in Chron. ad annum 414. scribit, Hac tempestate Pelagius Brito dogma nominis sui contra gratiam Christi exserit, praedicans, unumquemque ad justitiam propria voluntate regi, tantamque accipere gratiam quantum meruerit. Jam pro Semipelagianis loquatur Faustus illorum antesignanus, Attrahentis Dei misericordia si dignis datur, advertis quia jam et studio humanae utcunque servitutis impenditur, Lib. 1. cap. 17. Paulo post, In quem perspicis attrahentem, requirit omnimodis praecepta servantem, ut per quandam voluntatis ansulam comprehendi valeat qui vocatur.
pass_a: So concerning Pelagius himself Augustine writes that he held that God gives this grace unto him who shall have been worthy to receive it, Cap. 14. De gestis Palaestinis. And Haer. 88. the same Father witnesses that the Pelagians’ error was, That the grace of God by which we are freed from impiety is given according to our merits. So also Prosper in the Chronicle at the year 414. writes, In this season Pelagius the Briton puts forth the dogma of his name against the grace of Christ, preaching that each one is ruled unto righteousness by his own will, and receives as much grace as he shall have deserved. Now let Faustus their leader speak for the Semipelagians, If the mercy of the attracting God is given unto the worthy, you mark that it is already also spent upon the endeavour of human service somehow, Lib. 1. cap. 17. A little after, In him whom you see attracting, he requires in every way one keeping the precepts, that by a certain little handle of will he who is called may be able to be grasped.
pass_b: So Augustine on Pelagius himself (De gestis Palaestinis 14): he held God gives this grace to whoever is worthy to receive it. And Haeresis 88: the Pelagian error was that the grace by which we are freed from impiety is given according to our merits. Prosper’s Chronicle for 414: in that season Pelagius the Briton put forth his dogma against Christ’s grace, preaching that each is ruled to righteousness by his own will and receives as much grace as he deserves. For the Semipelagians hear their leader Faustus (lib. 1, c. 17): If the attracting God’s mercy is given to the worthy, you see it is already also spent on somehow serving by human effort. A little later: in the one you see attracting, he requires in every way a keeper of the precepts, so that by a little handle of will the called may be grasped.

lemmas.gloss: Pelagius: grace to the worthy/by merits
Faustus: attracting mercy if to the worthy

title: Cap. X Ultimum Propos. 3: ‘merit’ here means any prior better operation/disposition for which grace is given to one not another — then Fathers deny such prerequisite (Aug. contra 2 Epist. Pelag.)
latin: In hisce omnibus illud velim observetis, Ne ipsum quidem Pelagium negare gratiam offerri promiscue omnibus, dignis et indignis, ex miseratione Divina: sed in eo a Catholicis diversus abit, quod conferri eam semper et donari putet ex merito quodam speciali eorum quibus donatur, sicuti non dari ex demerito quodam speciali eorum quibus negatur. Meriti vero vocabulum apud Patres in hac controversia nil aliud sonat, quam antecedaneam operationem quamlibet aut dispositionem meliorem in uno quam alio, cujus intuitu datur haec gratia Christi uni et non alii. 2. Veritas praedictae nostrae propositionis inde liquet, quod Patres orthodoxi expresse negant, gratiam hanc salvantem praerequirere meliorem operationem aut conditionem ejus cui donatur, quam est eorum quibus non donatur: sed quicquid discriminis est inter homines, id effectum hujus gratiae acceptae, non causam motivam accipiendae, profitentur.
pass_a: In all these I would have you observe, That not even Pelagius himself denies that grace is offered promiscuously unto all, worthy and unworthy, from Divine pity: but in this he goes diverse from the Catholics, that he thinks it always conferred and given from some special merit of those unto whom it is given, just as not given from some special demerit of those unto whom it is denied. But the word merit in the Fathers in this controversy sounds nothing other than any antecedent operation or better disposition in one than in another, at the regard of which this grace of Christ is given unto one and not unto another. 2. The truth of our foresaid proposition is hence plain, that the orthodox Fathers expressly deny that this saving grace prerequires a better operation or condition of him unto whom it is given than is of those unto whom it is not given: but whatever discrimination there is among men, they profess to be the effect of this grace received, not the motive cause of receiving it.
pass_b: In all this mark: not even Pelagius denies grace is offered promiscuously to all, worthy and unworthy, from divine pity. He parts from the catholics in thinking it is always conferred from some special merit of those who receive it, and withheld from some special demerit of those denied it. In the Fathers here ‘merit’ means only any prior act or better disposition in one than another, with regard to which this Grace of Christ is given to one and not another. Second, our proposition’s truth is plain because the orthodox Fathers expressly deny that this saving grace prerequires a better act or condition in the receiver than in those not given it: whatever discrimination there is among men they profess as the effect of this grace received, not the motive cause of receiving it.

lemmas.lemma: effectum hujus gratiae ... non causam motivam
lemmas.gloss: person-difference is effect not motive of grace
